cards.title: Platform lift tests vs geo-lift tests: choosing your incrementality method
cards.summary: Compare in-platform lift experiments and geo-lift experiments on speed, cost, verifiability, and effort so you pick the right one for your paid media validation.
cards.use_when: You need to validate whether a paid channel (Meta, TikTok, Google, YouTube) is driving genuinely incremental purchases rather than just claiming credit for existing demand.
steps: Understand the in-platform lift test mechanism: the platform splits users individually into a treatment bucket (sees ads) and control bucket (no ads), then measures purchase behavior via pixel and computes incremental impact.
Know the in-platform lift pros: fast, can run continuously (Meta allows always-on runs), and works at individual user level so no country splitting is needed.
Know the in-platform lift cons: you rely entirely on the platform's data science and cannot verify their math or see raw data; it also depends on attribution being accurate.
Know geo-lift pros: you control the experimental design, own all the data, and can verify everything end-to-end.
Know geo-lift cons: slow to run, requires large spend to reach statistical significance, and requires holding variables constant across states and the test period.
Watch for minimum spend hurdles: the source notes TikTok (and similarly Google) may require roughly $200k spend before you can actually run the test; verify current platform minimums.
Source position: use both methods in one experiment design strategy rather than treating either as a silver bullet.

Ecommerce application: for a store deciding whether to keep or scale a channel, run a platform lift test when budget is limited and speed matters, and reserve geo-lift tests for high-revenue scenarios where you need verifiable causation.
caveats: Platform lift experiments cannot be independently verified — you trust the vendor's readout.
Geo-lift tests require large budgets and long timelines and are not easy to run.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Using causal impact / counterfactual modeling for retroactive channel analysis
cards.summary: Apply Google's open-source causal impact package to retrospectively estimate what revenue would have been without a channel intervention, using third-party confounding variables.
cards.use_when: You introduced a channel or campaign (e.g., YouTube, TikTok) at some point in the past and want a directional retrospective read on whether it actually drove revenue.
steps: Recognize the core problem: with no geo split you cannot prove causation, so you use a predictive model to build a counterfactual of what revenue would have been absent the intervention.
Identify predictive confounding variables for your daily revenue, such as ad spend, keyword seasonality, influencer spend, and inflation data.
Load those variables plus the intervention point into Google's open-source causal impact package (the source misspoke initially as 'causal inference').
Read the output as a predicted counterfactual revenue line versus actual revenue; the gap over the period is your directional incremental impact.
Apply the pack to real decisions: the source's example found an extra ~$10k revenue against $10k ad spend — roughly a 1x ROI — showing the channel was far less effective than assumed.
Use it as an add-on to your tooling to go back and analyze a past TikTok, YouTube, or similar launch.
Ecommerce application: before reallocating budget to a channel you launched during a strong season, run this analysis to avoid crediting the channel for what seasonality or spend already drove.
caveats: Causal impact is a predictive model using third-party variables, not true experimental proof — treat it as directional only.
It is Bayesian/statistical inference, not a substitute for a real geo-lift experiment when causation matters.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Why launch timing confuses channel results (Black Friday and Q4 era)
cards.summary: Brands wrongly credit a new channel for a strong period because they launched it during seasonality peaks without any measurement system.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to keep a channel you launched in October/November or during any peak season based on a good subsequent month.
steps: Identify the trap: introducing YouTube, TikTok, or another channel in October and then seeing a strong November leads many to assume the channel worked.
Ask how the uplift was actually measured — the source notes most cannot answer this; there is no test design, only correlation drawn from a good period.
Recognize that 'revenue went up after we launched' is not evidence the campaign caused it when seasonality is a strong confounding variable.
Demand a causal experimental design before treating the channel as a winner; without it, you may find your assumptions are wrong.

Ecommerce application: for a store planning a new channel launch, avoid launching it into peak season or, if you must, build the counterfactual model before drawing conclusions about its incremental value.
caveats: The source example is illustrative, not a quantified benchmark.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Setting up Conversions API (CAPI) on Meta for better tracking and optimization
cards.summary: Route purchase events server-side through Meta's Conversions API to bypass unreliable browser tracking and improve event matching and optimization.
cards.use_when: You are auditing or fixing Meta ad tracking for an ecommerce store and want to improve data quality feeding the ad platform.
steps: Install the Conversions API (CAPI) on Meta; the source says to make sure it is set up and working.
Understand the mechanism: instead of purchase events firing from the browser pixel, they fire on your own local server, which then reroutes them to Meta.
Know why it matters: this removes reliance on the browser, which is unreliable due to iOS changes, ad blockers, and privacy regulations.
Understand the matching benefit: CAPI passes back first-party data (email, phone number, customer ID), all hashed/privatized, which improves event match rates.
Use it for offline conversions: if someone buys in store using an email or phone, CAPI can link that purchase back to an ad served on the platform.
Accept the optimization payoff: better tracking means more data flowing into the platform, which improves ad optimization.
Ecommerce application: prioritize CAPI setup before scaling Meta spend, since poor tracking degrades optimization for every campaign you run.
caveats: Tool interfaces and setup steps change over time — verify current Meta CAPI setup instructions.
The source says brands doing $10-20M+/year should already have tracking configured, so this is more of a check than a from-scratch rebuild at that scale.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Avoid Shopify marketing/attribution reports for decisions
cards.summary: The source finds Shopify's marketing and attribution reports unreliable and recommends not using them for business decisions.
cards.use_when: You are setting up your measurement stack for an ecommerce store and deciding which data sources to trust for spend and revenue decisions.
steps: Do not rely on Shopify's marketing or attribution reports for decision-making; the source says it has rarely seen helpful data there.
Recognize this is fundamentally the same attribution problem you face elsewhere — the attribution models in Shopify are not reliable for understanding true impact.
Instead, build your decision dashboard on financial-based KPIs and platform data, not Shopify's attribution models.
Use G4 and Shopify only as needed; the source treats them as secondary or redundancy layers rather than primary decision dashboards.
Ecommerce application: when deciding budget shifts between channels, pull the numbers from your own incrementality testing and financial KPIs rather than the Shopify attribution report.
caveats: The source's assessment is as of May 2026 and reflects its own client experience — verify whether Shopify has updated its reporting.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Treat GA4 as a redundancy layer, not a daily decision dashboard
cards.summary: GA4 should collect data properly as a fallback, but should not drive day-to-day ecommerce decisions because it offers nothing you can't get from Shopify or the ad platforms.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what to actually open each day to make budget and campaign decisions for your store.
steps: Position GA4 as a redundancy layer: if your platform tracking breaks, GA4 gives quick directional insight as a fallback.
Ensure GA4 is set up properly — firing correctly, with campaigns segmented — so the fallback data has been collecting all along.
Do not use GA4 as your primary daily decision dashboard; the source says there is nothing in GA4 you cannot get from Shopify or the ad platforms.
Prioritize more important financial and incrementality metrics for indexing against your decisions instead.

Ecommerce application: for daily budget or scaling calls, work from new-customer revenue, acquisition CAC, and profit contribution dashboards; keep GA4 configured only so it is there when you need a backup read.
caveats: Source opinion as of May 2026; GA4 capabilities may change — verify before relying on this.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: One-day view attribution overattribution mistake
cards.summary: Running one-day view through all campaigns inflates reported ROAS with massive overattribution, so remove it to see reality.
cards.use_when: You are auditing Meta (or similar) campaign reporting and wondering why reported ROAS looks great but the business results disagree.
steps: Check whether one-day view attribution is enabled across all campaigns and being used in reporting.
Recognize this causes massive overattribution — the source cites 30-50% of reported ROAS coming from view-throughs.
Remove one-day view from reporting to get a more realistic read of what is actually occurring in the business.
Ecommerce application: before scaling budget on the strength of reported ROAS, strip view-through attribution and recalculate so your scaling decisions are based on real impact.
caveats: The 30-50% figure is the source's observation from audits, not a universal benchmark.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Account for Google's halo effect when judging ROAS
cards.summary: Google overattributes by taking credit for conversions that other platforms drove, so its ROAS should be reconsidered with skepticism.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating a PMax or Google campaign showing very high ROAS and deciding whether to increase spend.
steps: Understand the halo effect: Google's reported ROAS looks better than reality because it absorbs credit for what other platforms drove.
Do not conclude Google cannot acquire new customers — the source says you can profitably spend $100-200k/month on Google, but only if it is genuinely net incremental.

Stress-test the number: if a PMax campaign (even with brand excluded) shows 20x ROAS, skeptically consider putting an extra $1,000 in and checking whether you actually get $20,000 back in topline — likely you will not.
Treat Google's incrementality as usually overstated and account for the halo when reporting.
Ecommerce application: when deciding to scale Google spend for your store, validate with an incrementality test rather than trusting reported ROAS.
caveats: High Google ROAS is not proof of no incremental value — it means the reported figure overstates incremental impact.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Brand spend waste caused by over-prioritizing ROAS
cards.summary: Chasing ROAS as the north star leads accounts to leave brand search in, causing large waste even at 8-figure retailers.
cards.use_when: You are structuring paid search or campaign budgets and deciding whether to suppress brand terms.
steps: Recognize why brand waste happens: because ROAS is the north star metric, teams leave brand in to keep ROAS high.
Note the source sees this even in large 8-figure retailers, causing significant waste within the account.
Exclude brand where it is not genuinely incremental, and minimize brand search spend in your account structure.
Ecommerce application: in a store's paid search budget, separate brand and non-brand, and do not let brand conversions inflate the portfolio ROAS that justifies further spend.
caveats: Brand terms are not always non-incremental; the source's point is that ROAS-driven incentives cause over-investment in them.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Over-segmentation causes measurement fragmentation
cards.summary: Too many campaigns relative to business complexity and spend fragments data and makes decision-making convoluted.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing account structure and considering splitting campaigns further, or auditing why reporting is hard to interpret.
steps: Check whether your number of campaigns is disproportionate to your business complexity or spend level.
Understand the compounding effect: over-segmentation fragments data, which creates a measurement problem.
Recognize that with fragmented data, decision-making becomes very convoluted.
Consolidate campaigns to match business complexity and spend level to keep data readable.
Ecommerce application: for a store running many campaigns with modest budgets, simplify account structure so measurement and decisions stay clear rather than splitting further.
caveats: Over-segmentation is a judgment call; there is no fixed campaign count — assess against business complexity and spend.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Beware overattribution on low-spend tertiary channels
cards.summary: Small third-party channels like Snapchat, Pinterest, and Reddit show inflated ROAS because low spend defaults to reaching warm pixel audiences rather than driving new growth.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether a small tertiary channel's high ROAS justifies keeping or growing it.
steps: Identify the tertiary channels: Snapchat, Pinterest, Reddit, and similar channels with very low spend allocation.
Understand the mechanism: at low spend, the algorithm prioritizes the warm audience already hitting your site (with pixel) rather than new users.
Recognize the result: incredibly high reported ROAS on channels that are not actually driving new incremental growth.
Treat these high ROAS numbers with skepticism before crediting them for growth or scaling them.
Ecommerce application: for a store testing a small channel, measure new-customer impact or run an incrementality test rather than trusting the channel's reported ROAS.
caveats: The overattribution problem is driven by low spend, so larger budgets on these channels may behave differently and should be tested.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Stop existing-customer overspend that inflates metrics
cards.summary: Spending more on existing customers because ROAS looks good inflates all numbers and drives further misallocation.
cards.use_when: You are setting campaign objectives and budgets and need to decide whether to exclude existing customers.
steps: Look for budget increases justified by strong ROAS that are actually driven by existing-customer spend.
Recognize this inflates all the numbers and leads teams to increase budgets further based on misleading ROAS.
Exclude existing customers from top-of-funnel campaigns so results reflect acquisition.
Ecommerce application: in a store's prospecting campaigns, suppress past purchasers so reported returns reflect new-customer acquisition rather than repeat buyers who would have purchased anyway.
caveats: Excluding existing customers is specific to top-of-funnel campaigns; retention campaigns intentionally target them.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Top-funnel Meta objectives (traffic/reach) need a measurement system
cards.summary: Running traffic or reach campaigns on Meta without any measurement system means unmeasurable spend and false confidence drawn from correlation.
cards.use_when: You are considering traffic or reach campaigns for your store, or auditing whether existing ones are justified.
steps: Recognize that traffic/reach campaigns have no ROAS, which is why they are often run on assumed performance.
Understand the typical failure: almost no one running traffic campaigns has a way to actually measure their impact — they attribute revenue lift to correlation from agency reporting.
Evaluate the source's critique: running a traffic campaign at 3% of budget during Black Friday has essentially no measurable impact, and before/after correlation cannot prove it did.
Choose one path: if you run traffic or reach campaigns, fine, but have a measurement system (e.g., lift study or causal impact) in place to validate them.
Otherwise, do not run spend you cannot measure — the source's position is it is just wasting budget on something unvalidated.
Ecommerce application: for a store testing awareness-style objectives, predefine the lift test or counterfactual method before launching, not after.
caveats: This is the source's strong position that unmeasured top-funnel spend is not worth running; it does not forbid these objectives, it demands measurement.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: DPA overspend driven by attractive ROAS
cards.summary: Scaling dynamic product ads because ROAS looks good leads to non-incremental spend since DPAs sit at the bottom of funnel.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to increase DPA budget based on strong reported ROAS.
steps: Identify the pattern: DPAs show attractive ROAS, prompting people to spend more and more.
Recognize this is not actually incremental because DPAs sit at the bottom of the funnel and harvest existing demand.
Apply the same skepticism you use for brand and retargeting when reviewing DPA returns.
Ecommerce application: for a store scaling catalog/DPA campaigns, validate incrementality before raising budget rather than scaling purely on ROAS.
caveats: Bottom-funnel campaigns can still be valuable for conversion; the warning is against treating their ROAS as evidence of incremental growth.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Build a measurement and testing structure so every decision is validated
cards.summary: Without a testing/experimental design, you cannot validate whether anything is working, which the source considers a core scaling failure.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or auditing the measurement foundation for a store's paid media and need to decide what to test and how.
steps: Recognize the core diagnosis: most brands that fail to scale paid media have a measurement problem, not a paid media problem.
Understand the consequence: they optimize to numbers that do not match what is actually occurring in the business.
Establish a testing or experimental design before running any new initiative — if you cannot validate whether something works, the source argues it is not worth doing.
Connect this to the traffic/reach campaign problem: running something with no measurement system means you are just making assumptions.
Ecommerce application: for a store, define what outcome each new channel or campaign is meant to drive and the method (lift study, geo-lift, causal impact) that will validate it before spending.
caveats: The source's framing ('if you can't validate it, there's no point') is a strong position; smaller stores may still run low-cost exploratory spend.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Action items for $1-5M revenue stores: fix reporting basics
cards.summary: At $1-5M revenue, switch to 7-day click on Meta, tag COGS in Shopify, build a profit-focused dashboard, and exclude existing customers from top-of-funnel.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce store in the $1-5M revenue range and want the right baseline measurement actions.
steps: Switch to 7-day click reporting on Meta — the source says it correlates much better to acquisition metrics in the business.
Tag up Shopify cost of goods on all products so you get real-time visibility into gross margin.
Set up a dashboard giving a daily read on: acquisition new-customer profit contribution, new-customer revenue, new-customer orders, and blended CAC.
Exclude existing customers from top-of-funnel campaigns.
Minimize brand search spend.
Ecommerce application: implement these as the foundation for a store at this revenue level before layering in more advanced incrementality testing.
caveats: These are revenue-band heuristics from the source, not proven thresholds; apply based on your actual situation.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Action items for $5-20M revenue stores: layer in lift studies
cards.summary: At $5-20M revenue, add in-platform lift studies for top-funnel experimentation and use incremental attribution as a second validation layer beyond 7-day click.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce store in the $5-20M revenue range and have the basics in place, ready to add validation infrastructure.
steps: Retain all the $1-5M basics (7-day click, COGS tagging, profit dashboard, existing-customer exclusion, brand minimization).
Start layering in lift studies within the platforms.
Run top-funnel experimentation measured against those lift studies.
Use incremental attribution as a second validation layer beyond 7-day click reporting.
Ecommerce application: for a store at this scale, use lift studies to validate top-funnel spend that ROAS cannot measure, feeding incrementality factors back into reporting.
caveats: Revenue bands are source heuristics, not fixed rules; also note in-platform lift studies cannot be independently verified.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Action items for $20M+ revenue stores: geo-lift tests and incrementality factors
cards.summary: At $20M+, run geo-lift tests outside the platform and apply resulting incrementality factors to attributed ROAS numbers for a realistic view.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce store at $20M+ revenue with a complex channel and revenue capture mix and need verifiable incrementality measurement.
steps: Run geo-lift tests outside the platform for channels where you need verifiable causation.
Build a dashboard that pulls in omnichannel metrics from every revenue capture place, not just platform data.
Add one or two additional metrics on top of the baseline dashboard as your scale allows.

Apply incrementality factors: when a geo-lift gives an incremental return output, use it as a factor applied to in-platform attributed ROAS numbers to get a more realistic incremental view across campaigns and platforms.
Run consistent geo-lift tests at high frequency so you can derive incrementality factors across all channels and campaign types.
Ecommerce application: for a large store making big budget allocations, use these factors to correct platform ROAS before reallocating spend.
caveats: Requires very high frequency testing to build factors across all channels; geo-lift tests take significant time and spend.
Revenue bands are source heuristics.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Shift from ROAS to financial-based KPIs for scaling decisions
cards.summary: The source argues winning brands move toward financial-based KPIs and incrementality testing rather than optimizing to platform ROAS.
cards.use_when: You are setting the north-star metric for your store's paid media and deciding what to optimize.
steps: Identify the trap: optimizing to numbers that do not match what is actually occurring in the business, often ROAS inflated by view-throughs, brand, and bottom-funnel capture.
Understand the consequences chain: a measurement problem drives bad decision-making loops, and brands attribute credit to the wrong funnel stage.
Move toward financial-based KPIs (e.g., new-customer profit contribution, blended CAC, incremental return) rather than platform-reported ROAS as the north star.
Add incrementality tests at larger revenue levels to validate those financial KPIs.
At any level, prioritize cleaning up in-platform reporting as the first step.
Ecommerce application: for a store deciding where to scale, base the call on new-customer profit and CAC rather than a reported ROAS that may overattribute.
caveats: This is the source's strategic opinion, framed as where winning brands are headed in 2026-2027; the source also has a commercial interest in providing audits.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx
